cls: Atypical (second-generation) antipsychotic; major active metabolite of risperidone (benzisoxazole)
pharm: Combined central dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptor antagonism
tags: BOXED WARNING: increased mortality in elderly with dementia-related psychosis
Largely renally excreted - renal dosing matters
quick: Schizophrenia/schizoaffective: 6 mg once daily (range 3-12 mg/day); max 12 mg/day
May be taken with or without food (be consistent); swallow whole
Avoid unless necessary; 3rd-trimester neonatal EPS/withdrawal risk
Reduce dose: max 6 mg/day if CrCl 50-79; max 3 mg/day if CrCl 10-49; not recommended <10 mL/min
Mild-moderate (Child-Pugh A/B): no adjustment; not studied in severe
Metabolic (weight/glucose/lipids), prolactin if symptomatic, ECG/QT, EPS/tardive dyskinesia, renal function
summary: Paliperidone is the major active metabolite of risperidone, formulated as an OROS extended-release tablet for once-daily treatment of schizophrenia (adults and adolescents 12-17) and schizoaffective disorder (adults, alone or with mood stabilisers/antidepressants). The usual dose is 6 mg/day (range 3-12 mg). It is largely excreted unchanged by the kidneys, so dose reduction is required in renal impairment. Like other antipsychotics it carries a BOXED WARNING for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis (not an approved use), strongly raises prolactin, and can prolong the QT interval. The non-deformable tablet shell is excreted intact in stool.
indications: Schizoaffective disorder in adults - as monotherapy and as adjunct to mood stabilisers and/or antidepressants

dosage.d: 6 mg once daily; range 3-12 mg/day; max 12 mg/day
dosage.t: Initial titration not required; if increasing, raise by 3 mg/day at intervals >5 days
dosage.n: Doses >6 mg weighed against dose-related adverse reactions

dosage.d: Start 3 mg/day; <51 kg max 6 mg/day, >=51 kg max 12 mg/day
dosage.t: Increase by 3 mg/day at intervals >5 days

dosage.d: 6 mg once daily; range 3-12 mg/day; max 12 mg/day
dosage.n: Monotherapy or adjunct to mood stabiliser/antidepressant

admin: Swallow the ER tablet whole with liquid; do not chew, divide, or crush
May be taken with or without food, but keep timing consistent
Take at approximately the same time each day (morning preferred to limit insomnia)
The tablet shell does not dissolve - it is eliminated intact in the stool (harmless)
Avoid in patients with severe pre-existing GI narrowing
moa: Paliperidone is the principal active metabolite of risperidone (9-hydroxyrisperidone). Its therapeutic effect in schizophrenia is thought to be mediated through combined antagonism of central dopamine type-2 (D2) and serotonin type-2A (5-HT2A) receptors. It also has antagonist activity at alpha1- and alpha2-adrenergic and H1-histaminergic receptors, accounting for orthostatic hypotension and sedation. D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway elevates prolactin. The OROS delivery system provides a controlled, gradually rising release over 24 hours, minimising peak-trough fluctuation.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to paliperidone or risperidone, or to any tablet excipient (reactions including anaphylaxis and angioedema reported)
relative: Elderly with dementia-related psychosis (BOXED WARNING - increased mortality and cerebrovascular events)
Known cardiovascular/cerebrovascular disease or conditions predisposing to hypotension
Congenital long QT, history of arrhythmia, or concomitant QT-prolonging drugs
Pre-existing severe GI narrowing (non-deformable ER tablet)
Conditions associated with elevated prolactin / prolactin-dependent tumours

preg: Antipsychotics including paliperidone may cause extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, hypertonia/hypotonia, tremor, somnolence, respiratory distress, feeding difficulty) in neonates exposed during the third trimester. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Monitor exposed neonates. There is a pregnancy registry for antipsychotic exposure.
lact: Paliperidone is excreted in human breast milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the breastfed infant, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, weighing benefits of breastfeeding and the mother's clinical need.
renal: Paliperidone is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidneys, so dose reduction is required in renal impairment. For mild impairment (CrCl 50 to <80 mL/min): initial 3 mg/day, maximum 6 mg/day. For moderate-to-severe impairment (CrCl 10 to <50 mL/min): initial 1.5 mg/day, maximum 3 mg/day. Use in patients with CrCl <10 mL/min has not been studied and is not recommended.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is required in mild to moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh class A and B). Paliperidone has not been studied in severe hepatic impairment.

major: Other QT-prolonging drugs (Class IA/III antiarrhythmics, some antipsychotics, certain antibiotics) - additive QT risk
Centrally acting drugs and alcohol (additive CNS depression)
Levodopa and dopamine agonists (paliperidone antagonises their effect)
moderate: Strong P-gp inducers e.g. carbamazepine, rifampin (may reduce paliperidone exposure)
Risperidone co-administration (paliperidone is risperidone's metabolite - avoid combining)
minor: CYP enzyme inhibitors/inducers have limited effect (paliperidone is minimally metabolised)
interactions.food: A high-fat/high-calorie meal can increase paliperidone exposure; take consistently with respect to food
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive sedation and CNS depression
interactions.diagnostics: Raises serum prolactin (may interfere with prolactin-dependent diagnostics); may prolong ECG QT interval

emergency: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, raised CPK)

monitoring: Fasting glucose/HbA1c and lipids at baseline and periodically (metabolic effects)
Weight/BMI at baseline and during treatment
Prolactin level if symptoms of hyperprolactinaemia
ECG (QT) in patients with cardiac risk or on QT-prolonging drugs
Renal function (creatinine clearance) to guide dosing
Extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia
CBC during the first months if history of low WBC/neutropenia
Signs of NMS (fever, rigidity, altered mental status)
counsel: Swallow the tablet whole - do not chew, crush, or split it
You may notice the empty tablet shell in your stool; this is normal and harmless
May cause drowsiness and dizziness on standing - rise slowly; take care driving
Report fever with muscle stiffness or confusion urgently (NMS)
Report breast swelling/discharge, menstrual changes, or sexual problems (raised prolactin)
Tell your clinician about pregnancy, breastfeeding, kidney problems, diabetes, and all other medicines
Do not stop suddenly without medical advice
pk: Antipsychotic effect develops over days to weeks; gradual ER release over 24 h
Plasma Cmax approximately 24 hours after the dose
Supports once-daily dosing; steady state in 4-5 days
Store at 25 degrees C (excursions 15-30 degrees C); protect from moisture
pearls: BOXED WARNING: elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have increased mortality - paliperidone is NOT approved for this use.
Paliperidone is the active metabolite of risperidone (9-hydroxyrisperidone) - do not co-prescribe with risperidone.
Largely renally excreted with minimal hepatic metabolism, so renal function (not hepatic) drives dosing; CYP interactions are limited.
OROS non-deformable shell: counsel patients the empty 'ghost tablet' in stool is expected; avoid in severe GI narrowing.
Among the antipsychotics most likely to raise prolactin; monitor metabolic parameters as a class effect.
A separate long-acting injectable form (paliperidone palmitate) exists for monthly/3-monthly dosing - this record covers the oral ER tablet.
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two tablets at once to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Signs reflect exaggerated pharmacology: drowsiness, sedation, tachycardia, hypotension, QT prolongation, and extrapyramidal symptoms. There is no specific antidote. Manage with airway/ventilation support, continuous cardiac/ECG monitoring for arrhythmia and QT prolongation, IV fluids and sympathomimetics (avoid those with beta-stimulant activity that worsen hypotension) for circulatory support, and anticholinergics for severe EPS. Gastric lavage and activated charcoal may be considered. Close supervision until recovery.
